analysis.one_liner: Claws back private equity profits from failed health care takeovers and cuts off Medicare payments tied to real estate trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Maggie Goodlander on February 12, 2026, sits without a single cosponsor in three House committees and has seen no action since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets private equity firms that buy up hospitals, nursing homes, and medical practices. It would let the Justice Department and state attorneys general claw back money the owners took out of a health care company — through dividends, fees, or selling its buildings — for up to ten years before or after the company misses payroll, stops paying rent, or goes bankrupt, and it would add prison time of one to six years when patients are harmed. It would also cut off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell their buildings to real estate trusts, end tax breaks those trusts get on health care income, require yearly public reporting of who owns health care companies and how much debt they carry, and order a government study of profit-driven practices in medicine.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at private-equity-owned hospitals, nursing homes, and physician practices, who would gain protection when owners strip profits and the facility then misses payroll, stops paying rent, or goes bankrupt; health care workers and pensioners, who would be first in line for clawed-back money covering unpaid salaries, benefits, and pension shortfalls; and taxpayers, who would gain from ending special tax treatment of health care REIT income and from a public database of who owns and is levering up their local hospitals. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: When a health care company taken over by investors misses payroll for a quarter of its workers, stops paying rent or loans, closes, or files for bankruptcy, the government could claw back compensation the owners took out during the surrounding ten years — including salaries, bonuses, profits from asset sales, management and monitoring fees, and golden parachutes.

Money clawed back would go first to cover shortfalls in wages, benefits, and — in a bankruptcy — pension funds owed to the company's current and former employees, then to serve the health needs of the harmed community, rather than into the general treasury.
Owners who contributed to a triggering event that kills or injures patients could face one to six years in prison and a civil penalty of up to five times the clawback amount.

Medicare and Medicaid would stop paying providers that sell their buildings to, or pledge assets as collateral with, a real estate investment trust — cutting off a financing arrangement often used to strip equity from hospitals and nursing homes.

Health care entities would have to report ownership, mergers, debt levels, real estate leases, and payments to investors every year, and the Department of Health and Human Services would post the information on a public website, so patients and communities could see who owns and is leveraging their local providers.

The HHS Inspector General would study how profit-driven practices — upcoding, staffing cuts, restrictive insurer utilization reviews, and evasion of state corporate-practice-of-medicine laws — affect patient care, health workers, and public insurance programs, and estimate who profits from them.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms and their executives, whose profits from health care buyouts could be clawed back for up to a decade and who could face 1–6 years in prison; health care real estate investment trusts, which would lose Medicare and Medicaid revenue from newly sold or pledged hospital property and lose tax preferences on health care dividends; and large hospital systems and provider groups, which would bear the cost of annual ownership and debt reporting to the government. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity firms and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The clawback and criminal provisions are sweeping: a covered party's exposure is triggered by ordinary business distress like a 90-day rent or loan default, and covered compensation reaches as far as any profits from buying or selling assets, so executives and funds could owe back a decade of earnings without any finding of fraud — an affirmative defense only if they prove by clear and convincing evidence they could not prevent the event.

Banning Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that deal with real estate trusts is blunt: it could cut off a real financing channel that some hospitals and nursing homes rely on to raise capital, not just the exploitative sale-leaseback deals the bill targets.

The annual ownership reporting requirement covers even small physician-owned practices enrolled in Medicare, imposing new compliance costs across the sector, with penalties up to $5 million per missing or false report.
The bill has attracted no cosponsors, which means it has not been refined or tested against objections in any committee and is unlikely to become law in this Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a documented problem — private equity owners extracting dividends, fees, and real estate profits from health care companies that then miss payroll or go bankrupt — and its transparency and study provisions are low-cost, common-sense measures. But its enforcement core is designed broadly: criminal liability and ten-year clawbacks can attach to ordinary financial distress rather than proven misconduct, and the Medicare/Medicaid ban on REIT deals could restrict legitimate financing. As written, the deterrent value for patients and workers likely outweighs the risk to responsible investors, but the bill would need significant narrowing to pass — and with zero cosponsors, it has not even begun that process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, and since then nothing has happened: no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Maggie Goodlander introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, with no cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce — splitting it across the committees with power over taxes, criminal law, and health programs.
No committee has taken up the bill and no further action appears in the record since the day of introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet, because the bill has not advanced. Private equity firms and health care real estate trusts are better off so far only in the ordinary sense that a bill aimed at them has gained no cosponsors and no committee action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and REIT investors, so far

for.name: Rep. Maggie Goodlander
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on February 12, 2026; no other member has cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: So far the bill is entirely one-sided: a single first-term Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded opposition or support from any other member.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and their executives
industries.note: The bill is aimed squarely at private equity's health care playbook: it creates criminal exposure and a ten-year profit clawback triggered by missed payroll, unpaid rent, loan defaults, or bankruptcy, and it specifically targets dividend recapitalizations, sale-leaseback deals, and monitoring fees — the main ways owners extract cash from acquired providers.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts (REITs)
industries.note: Providers that sell buildings to, or pledge assets as collateral with, a REIT would be barred from Medicare and Medicaid, and REITs would lose favorable tax treatment of health care dividends, including the 20% pass-through deduction. This attacks the sale-leaseback model in which hospital operators sell their real estate to investors and lease it back at rising rents.

industries.industry: Hospitals, health systems, and consolidated provider groups
industries.note: Every Medicare-enrolled hospital, health system, physician practice, surgery center, hospice, and dialysis facility would have to report ownership, debt, leases, and payments to investors annually, with fines up to $5 million per false or missing report. Large chains absorb this as a compliance cost; some could also benefit if clawed-back funds shore up payrolls and pensions at distressed facilities.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no hearings, and no movement in any of its three committees months after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to advance. Most House bills introduced by a single member die in committee without a hearing or a vote, and nothing in the record so far separates this one from that pattern.
